about.title: About being a companion
about.sees: You only see what {name} chose to share — never her cycle history, private notes or the details of what she logs.
about.words: Everything is written in probabilistic words, because everyone's experience is different. The best way to know how she feels is to ask her.
about.control: {name} can change what you see or end the link at any time.

menstrual.main: She's probably on her period these days.
menstrual.sub: Her body may want more rest and calm, but everyone's experience is different.

follicular.main: She's probably in the first half of her cycle.
follicular.sub: For many people these days feel a little lighter, but everyone's experience is different.

fertile.main: She's probably in the middle of her cycle.

luteal.main: She's probably in the second half of her cycle.
luteal.sub: She may feel a bit more tired or want more rest these days, but everyone's experience is different.

pregnancy.sub: Every day of a pregnancy can feel different — the best way to know is to ask her.

learn.title: Learn
learn.heading: Better support, with a little knowledge
learn.sub: Short, simple reads — no medical or definitive language.
learn.disclaimer: These notes are general and educational and don't replace advice from a professional.

myths.title: Common myths about periods and mood
myths.body: Not every change in how someone feels is “because of her period”; pinning a person's behaviour on her cycle is neither accurate nor respectful. Her feelings are as real as anyone else's. Everyone's experience is their own.

cycle.body: The menstrual cycle is a natural, repeating process that usually lasts a few weeks and has several phases. Its length, and how each phase feels, varies from person to person and even month to month. Ritme only shows a general, probabilistic picture of the phase, never a certain prediction. The best source on how she feels is her.

support.body: Supporting someone means being there without shrinking or inflating what they feel. Lines like “it must be your period” don't help and can hurt. Instead of guessing, ask what would help and respect the answer. Sometimes knowing you're there is enough.

space.long: When to ask, when to give space
space.body: Nobody wants to talk all the time, and that's completely normal. A simple “Would you like to talk, or have some time alone?” lets her choose. If she wants space, stepping back gently is support too. Check in again later, without pushing.

empathy.body: When someone shares something hard, they often want to be heard first, not handed a fix. Empathy is saying “that sounds hard” and letting them finish. If you're unsure, ask: “Do you want me to just listen, or think it through together?” Solutions help when she asks for them.

personal.sub: Let's learn something new about being a good companion today.

tips.listen: You don't always have to “fix” things — sometimes simply listening is the best support.
tips.ask: Ask instead of guessing; a kind question beats any assumption.
tips.small: Small, steady gestures often mean more than one big one.
tips.space: Sometimes support means giving space; respecting “not now” is care too.
tips.notice: Notice the small things that lift the people close to you, and remember them.
tips.together: A simple shared plan, even a short one, can lift you both.
tips.patience: Every day is different from the last; be patient with yourself and others.
